studies.label: Study 1 (broad startup idea task, master's students)

counts_source.quote: Ninety-three participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: exposed to ideas generated by a fine-tuned LLM (n = 46) or no exposure to LLM-generated ideas (n = 47). ... In total, 90 participants (45 per group)

arms.name: LLM-assisted human
arms.description: Shown 10 ideas randomly drawn from a database of 453 GPT-3 startup ideas, told they were generated by artificial intelligence, free to use them as inspiration but not to suggest an identical idea; told they could do some internet research (Appendix B, p. 14)

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Same scenario, instructions and Qualtrics interface with no AI-generated ideas; told they could do some internet research, as in the AI arm (same interface: p. 7, Section 4.2; instructions: Appendix B, p. 14)

studies.task: Generate startup ideas in any domain for an incubator, specifying the business need, product or service, revenue source and target customer; instructions allow approximately 10 minutes with an 8-minute minimum (PDF pp. 7-8; PDF p. 14, Appendix B).

ai_tool.name: GPT-3 via Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI (ideasai.net), described as fine-tuned

preregistration.where: No preregistration is mentioned in the full document; an a priori power analysis is described on PDF p. 6, Section 4.1, and referenced on PDF p. 9, Section 5.1.

estimates.outcome: Breadth of exploration (semantic categories per participant)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Number of distinct semantic categories represented in each participant's ideas. An author developed the coding scheme and an independent researcher reviewed and coded ideas; scores were averaged across raters. Study 1 uses 15 categories (PDF p. 7, Section 4.4.1; Appendix C, PDF pp. 15-16).

sources.locator: PDF p. 9, Table 4, Breadth of Exploration (columns M, SD, N, d)
sources.quote: Breadth of Exploration LLM-assisted human 2.32 1.32 45 0.67 Human-only 1.60 0.74 45
breadth of exploration (χ2(1) = 6.43, p = 0.01)
In total, 90 participants (45 per group) generated 208 ideas.

estimates.notes: Kruskal-Wallis test reported with a chi-squared statistic. The paper says parametric tests give similar conclusions but prints no separate parametric statistics. Cohen's d is transcribed as printed; its standardizer is not specified. This is the hypothesized, paper-primary outcome; no preregistration is stated. Per the reconciled form and codebook primary-record rule, prefer breadth for with_ai over the secondary expert creativity rating. The paper states that this result remains significant after Holm–Bonferroni correction for the two primary outcome tests; it prints no separate adjusted p-value.

estimates.outcome: Depth of exploration (ideas per explored semantic category)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Number of ideas generated divided by breadth of exploration for each participant; a measure of concentration within explored categories, interpreted as a consequence of cognitive persistence (PDF p. 8, Section 4.4.2).

sources.quote: Depth of Exploration LLM-assisted human 1.13 0.26 45 0.07 Human-only 1.15 0.33 45
depth of exploration (χ2(1) = 0.45, p = 0.50)
In total, 90 participants (45 per group) generated 208 ideas.

estimates.notes: Kruskal-Wallis test reported with a chi-squared statistic. The paper says parametric tests give similar conclusions but prints no separate parametric statistics. Cohen's d is transcribed as printed; its standardizer is not specified. Higher values mean more ideas per explored category (greater within-category concentration), not an unambiguous improvement in creativity; higher_is is therefore other. This is an unhypothesized additional primary check and is not a pooling candidate. The positive d = 0.07 is retained although the AI-arm mean is lower than the control mean; no sign correction or recomputation was made.

estimates.outcome: Average within-condition cosine similarity between participants' ideas
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Average within-condition pairwise cosine similarity of SpaCy sentence embeddings; the embedding model is not named. Preprocessing includes tokenization, stop-word and generic-word removal, lemmatization, and punctuation removal. Study 1 retains only each participant's first idea (PDF p. 8, Section 4.6.2).

stats.difference_is: Human-only minus LLM-assisted human (control minus treatment), as printed; the narrative states human-only ideas are more similar.

sources.locator: PDF p. 11, Table 7, Study 1 rows (columns M, SD, N (ideas))
sources.quote: Cosine similarity | Study 1 LLM-assisted human | 0.74 | 0.13 | 45 | Study 1 Human-only | 0.81 | 0.08 | 45
(M differ­ ence = 0.07, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.04, 0.10], p = 0.00, Cohen's d = 0.91)
Based on permutation tests with 10,000 iterations
In total, 90 participants (45 per group) generated 208 ideas.

estimates.notes: Exploratory group-level similarity analysis. Permutation test with 10,000 iterations; no separate test statistic, degrees of freedom or SE is printed. Table 7 labels N as ideas, not pairs; participant counts are sourced separately. The number of pairs is not printed and is not computed. The SD level and Cohen's d standardizer are unspecified. se_basis is conservatively coded pair because the outcome is pairwise similarity and the paper does not establish the resampling unit or participant-level uncertainty; this coding must not be read as confirmation that individual pairs were permuted independently. The confidence interval and effect sign are retained in the paper's direction, without reversal or standardization. Lower similarity in the AI arm means greater across-person diversity. The printed p = 0.00 is retained as an exact printed value, not changed into a bound.

not_extracted.what: S1-O8: semantic similarity of the LLM-generated stimulus pool versus human-only ideas, including stimulus-pool cleaning diagnostics
not_extracted.reason: The stimulus-pool arm contains no person working with AI; this is AI output versus human output, outside extraction of randomized human-assistance contrasts. The before/after cleaning comparison is model-only (PDF p. 7, Section 4.2; PDF p. 8, Section 4.6.2).

not_extracted.what: S2-O8: semantic similarity of the LLM-generated education stimulus pool versus human-only ideas
not_extracted.reason: The pool consists of AI-generated stimuli, not output produced by participants under randomized assistance. The comparison is contextual AI-versus-human evidence and is excluded (PDF p. 10, Section 5.5.2).

not_extracted.what: Study 1 manipulation check: awareness that suggestions were AI-generated
not_extracted.reason: Self-reported awareness of the source, not a creativity outcome scored on participant output (PDF p. 7, Section 4.3).

not_extracted.what: Study 2 manipulation check: awareness that suggestions were AI-generated
not_extracted.reason: Self-reported awareness of the source, not a creativity outcome scored on participant output (PDF p. 9, Section 5.3).

not_extracted.what: Study 1 breadth comparisons by manipulation-check response and sensitivity analysis dropping incorrect responders
not_extracted.reason: Subgroup/nonrandom comparisons and a restricted-sample robustness check rather than a full-sample randomized contrast. Only qualitative conclusions are printed (PDF p. 7, Section 4.3).

not_extracted.what: Study 2 breadth comparisons by manipulation-check response and sensitivity analysis dropping incorrect responders
not_extracted.reason: Subgroup/nonrandom comparisons and a restricted-sample robustness check rather than a full-sample randomized contrast. Only qualitative conclusions are printed (PDF p. 9, Section 5.3).

The preliminary phases concern scenario feedback and refinement, not reported randomized AI-assistance comparisons on creative output; participants were excluded from the final experiment (PDF p. 7, Section 4.3).

not_extracted.what: Paper-level idea length/elaboration: AI-exposed participants produced shorter ideas on average
not_extracted.reason: Appendix D, PDF p. 19, Interpretation, presents this as a plausible explanation but provides no study attribution, length measure, analysis unit, sample count or numerical result. It cannot be assigned to a study-specific estimate without inventing provenance; the observation is retained here and as an open item.

not_extracted.what: Appendix C pooled semantic-category and sub-code frequencies
not_extracted.reason: These describe the combined idea pools and the coding schemes, without AI-versus-control arm statistics. They are not additional eligible contrasts (PDF pp. 15-18, Appendix C).

not_extracted.what: Appendix E Shapiro-Wilk normality tests and kernel-density plots for breadth and depth
not_extracted.reason: These are distributional diagnostics, not AI-versus-comparison effects. No values are read off the density plots (PDF p. 19, Appendix E).

open_items: Study 2 prints randomized counts for each arm but no combined randomized total (PDF p. 9, Section 5.1). The combined n_randomized field is null under the transcription-only rule; it has not been computed from the arm counts.

The similarity SDs in Table 7 are not assigned to pairs or participant/idea-level averages. The permutation unit and confidence-interval construction are not specified, so participant-level uncertainty cannot be confirmed. se_basis is provisionally pair, and sd_level is null (PDF pp. 8, 10-11).
Neither the main-outcome nor similarity Cohen's d standardizers are defined. Their printed signs and values are retained without assuming a pooled or control SD denominator (PDF pp. 8-11).

Study 2 similarity: the first-idea selection rule is not expressly repeated, and the subtraction order for the printed positive difference is unstated despite equal rounded arm means (PDF p. 10, Section 5.5.2; PDF p. 11, Table 7).
Study 1 usefulness and creativity: it is unclear whether the dropped third usefulness item enters the reported Study 1 scores (PDF p. 18, Appendix D).

Study 2 excludes task-unrelated ideas and participants, but the out-of-instruction-scope category remains in its taxonomy. The paper does not clarify whether that category enters main-analysis breadth (PDF p. 9, Sections 5.1 and 5.4; PDF p. 16, Appendix C).

Per-arm exclusions and reasons are not explicitly allocated; only arm randomized/analyzed counts and overall exclusion descriptions are available (PDF pp. 6, 8-9). No per-arm exclusion counts have been derived.
The country of recruitment for Study 1 is not stated; international student status and use of French do not establish country (PDF p. 6, Section 4.1).

Possible sample overlap with c917 (Sorin and Pagani, 2022, AOM abstract) or the cited Sorin and Pagani 2023 chapter remains unconfirmed. The reconciled form identifies these leads; the PDF acknowledges earlier AOM presentations but does not identify shared participants (PDF p. 13; chapter reference, PDF p. 20). shared_sample remains null.

The paper-level shorter-ideas statement needs study attribution, measurement details, sample/unit and numerical results before it can become an elaboration estimate (PDF p. 19, Appendix D, Interpretation).
notes: Extraction B completed from the published PDF and the complete markdown conversion, including appendices and references; all estimate numbers were checked in pymupdf page text. Figure 1 is a conceptual evidence diagram with no extractable numerical contrast; Appendix E plots are diagnostic. Eligible-statistic inventory: Tables 4 and 6 supply arm means, SDs, participant Ns and Cohen's d for breadth and depth, with Kruskal-Wallis statistics and p-values in Sections 4.6.1 and 5.5.1. Table 7 and Sections 4.6.2 and 5.5.2 supply similarity arm means/SDs, differences, confidence intervals, permutation p-values and Cohen's d. Appendix D supplies participant-level means, SDs and Ns for creativity, novelty, usefulness and idea count, without inferential tests. PDF and printed page numbers agree. Original decimal precision is retained in numeric JSON tokens and source quotes. No effects, SEs, count totals or confidence limits were computed. The source document names GPT-3 through its Brown et al. (2020) reference and cites the startup-idea product as 2022; year denotes the model, not data-collection year. Both studies used supplied static ideas before ChatGPT became available. The paper calls the generator fine-tuned, while Section 7 and Appendix A describe domain examples and feedback supplied through prompting. Both Study 1 arms could use internet research. Analyses omit non-completers in Study 1 and task-unrelated responses in Study 2. Study 2's unreported combined randomized count is not copied from the screening form. Paper-primary breadth takes precedence over the unhypothesized depth check and secondary Appendix D ratings; preregistered_primary remains not_stated because no registration is identified. No participant-level data were used; PDF p. 19 states that data are available on request. Shared samples are unconfirmed, as specified in the reconciled form.
